title: Arlette regarde une série  (Game of Thrones)

segments.t: We start at the agency with Arlette and Mathias. Listen to the whole scene in French first — don't worry if it goes by fast.
Cette actrice est tellement magnétique et élégante.
Elle est vraiment poétique aussi.
Ensuite, la petite femme devient aveugle.
Et la grande fille stupide meurt!
Arlette, tu regardes encore cette série?
Oui, la fin m'énerve beaucoup.
Peux-tu trouver la prochaine saison?

Let's examine how Arlette shares her passion for television with Mathias.
Cette actrice est tellement magnétique et élégante.
'That actress is so magnetic and elegant.' Arlette piles on two easy English cognates, linking them with an intensifier that means 'so' or 'to such a degree'.
Elle est vraiment poétique aussi.
'She is truly poetic as well.' Notice how 'also' tucks neatly onto the very end in French rather than sitting right after 'is'.
Ensuite, la petite femme devient aveugle.
'Then, the small woman becomes blind.' Opening with a handy word meaning 'next' or 'afterward' keeps a story moving from one twist to the next.
Et la grande fille stupide meurt!
'And the stupid tall girl dies!' One describing word stands before 'girl' for height while the insult comes after it, surrounding the person in French.
Arlette, tu regardes encore cette série?
'Arlette, are you still watching this series?' Mathias uses the casual 'you' with a colleague he knows well, and the word meaning 'still' can mean 'again' in other contexts.
Oui, la fin m'énerve beaucoup.
'Yes, the ending annoys me a lot.' Literally 'gets on my nerves', the action puts 'me' shortened to a single letter right before the vowel.
Peux-tu trouver la prochaine saison?
'Can you find the next season?' Flipping 'can' and casual 'you' builds a crisp question, though in relaxed speech you'll hear people keep normal statement order.
Un an, c'est trop long d'attendre.
'One year is too long to wait.' Naming 'one year' first and then echoing it with 'it is' gives the complaint punchy spoken rhythm in French.
C'est quoi le titre déjà?
'What is the title again?' Adding a word that usually means 'already' onto the end of a question is how you ask 'again?' when a detail slips your mind.
Tu vis dans une grotte, Mathias?
'Do you live in a cave, Mathias?' This teasing expression matches the English idiom almost word-for-word, using casual 'you' and rising pitch alone to ask.
C'est la célèbre série Game of Thrones.
'It is the famous series Game of Thrones.' Placing 'famous' ahead of 'series' lends dramatic flair, whereas many describing words in French follow what they describe.
Je verrai Louis Garrel au théâtre jeudi.
'I will see Louis Garrel at the theater Thursday.' Just as in English, the day of the week drops in bare at the end without needing 'on' before it.
Dis à Berléand que ses contrats sont prêts.
'Tell Berleand that his contracts are ready.' Where English says 'tell someone', French builds this command with 'say to' before the actor's surname.
Au fait, ton haut sent la friture.

'By the way, your top smells like frying.' Starting with a two-word chunk literally meaning 'at the fact' lets Mathias pivot smoothly, and 'smells the frying' needs no 'like'. Now let's listen to the whole humorous exchange between Arlette and Mathias again at full speed.

Arlette's obsession with fantasy television amuses the office, but Mathias remains strictly focused on client contracts. Their teasing dynamic highlights the lighthearted atmosphere at ASK before new challenges arrive. See you next time!
À demain!
